soil-agri-128.title: The three-field system: crops two years in three
soil-agri-128.text: An estate's arable land was split into three fields. In this crop rotation, a field grows one set of crops in the first year, a different set in the second, and lies fallow in the third. One field was sown in autumn with winter wheat or rye, one with peas, lentils or beans, and one was left fallow. The legumes fixed nitrogen that the cereals depleted, and livestock grazing the weedy fallow fertilized it with their excrement. Each field was cropped two years in three, whereas the older two-field system left half the land fallow. First used in China in the Eastern Zhou period, it spread in Europe from the 9th to the 11th century alongside the mouldboard plough. Summer-dry Mediterranean lands suited it less.

soil-agri-119.title: Controlling weeds when the plough stays out
soil-agri-119.text: Without tillage, something else has to kill the weeds. Weed management in no-till uses herbicides, cover plantings, mowing or crimping in place of cultivation. Herbicides such as glyphosate replace tillage for preparing the ground for seed, so no-till uses more herbicide than conventional tillage. Residue left on the surface can also bring different, greater or more frequent disease and weed problems than tilled fields have. Weed-suppressing cover plantings, described in {{ref:soil-agri-066}}, add organic residue but must be killed, typically by crimping at flowering, and the crop is planted through the remaining mulch. Herbicides are not strictly necessary, as natural farming and {{ref:soil-env-218}} show. Winter cover plantings, soil solarization and burning are alternatives.

soil-agri-127.title: Making unfarmable land grow crops
soil-agri-127.text: On the rocky Aran Islands off Ireland, people spread a shallow layer of seaweed and sand to grow crops. The islands still count as non-arable. Conversion to arable land means making land that cannot grow crops capable of cultivation. It may require irrigation canals, wells, desalination, fertilizer, pesticides, {{ref:soil-agri-061}} or heated greenhouses, and it is often prohibitively expensive. Slash-and-burn farming draws on nutrients in wood ash, but these are used up within a few years. Terra preta soils were made fertile by adding charcoal.

soil-agri-124.title: Keyline design: steering runoff so it soaks in
soil-agri-124.text: Even ordinary contour ploughing drifts off the contour, sending runoff off ridges and into valleys. Keyline design is P. A. Yeomans' system of planning farm landscapes around the natural flow of water, to make the best use of their water resources. The keyline is the contour through the keypoint, where a valley floor suddenly steepens. Cultivating parallel to it drifts runoff away from the valley center, delaying runoff concentration and giving water more time to infiltrate. Its Keyline Scale of Permanence orders farm elements from landshape and water supply through roads and structures to fences. Philipp Gerhardt's Seepage Line System replaces fixed keylines with custom contour ditches, and trials in Germany show it reduces surface runoff.

soil-agri-107.title: The ard, an ox-drawn scratch plough
soil-agri-107.text: Oxen domesticated in Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley, perhaps as early as the 6th millennium BC, supplied the draft power that made the ard possible. The ard is the early animal-drawn scratch plough, which drags a share, a cutting blade, through the topsoil to cut a shallow furrow. A ploughed field from about 2800 BCE has been found at Kalibangan, India. The ard left undisturbed strips between furrows, so fields were cross-ploughed both ways, which tended to form squarish Celtic fields. It suits loamy or sandy soils renewed by floods, as in the Nile Delta and Fertile Crescent, and it struggled in northern Europe's heavy soils.

soil-agri-111.title: The chisel plough, which loosens deep and leaves the cover
soil-agri-111.text: Most ploughs turn the soil over; the chisel plough does not. It is a plough for deep tillage that loosens and aerates soil while leaving crop residue on the surface. That suits no-till and low-till farming, and some consider it more sustainable than the mouldboard plough. It can reduce the effects of compaction and help break up hardpans, including {{ref:soil-agri-101}}. In essence it is a heavy-duty version of the tool in {{ref:soil-agri-115}}, working 15 cm to 46 cm deep. Each shank needs 10 to 20 horsepower (7.5 to 14.9 kW). The lighter tool's teeth work near the surface, mainly against weeds, so they need far less power per shank.

soil-agri-110.title: The heavy plough that made farming communal
soil-agri-110.text: Pulling a heavy plough took four to eight oxen, more than one peasant household had. So farming became communal, and the manorial system rose. The heavy plough was a wheeled plough heavy enough to carry a large metal-faced mould board, and so to work the heavy soils of northern Europe. By the Han period Chinese ploughshares were wholly cast iron, the earliest known heavy iron mould-board ploughs. In Europe, adoption of the carruca heavy plough accompanied the three-field system in the later 8th and early 9th centuries, raising yields per unit of land. Heavy ploughs raised food production, coinciding with a marked rise in world population in the second millennium AD.

soil-agri-108.title: Hoe cultivation, where farming began
soil-agri-108.text: Agriculture began with the digging stick and the hoe. Hoe cultivation is turning soil with these hand-held tools. In very fertile areas such as the Nile banks, renewed by the annual flood, hoes cut furrows for seeds. Digging sticks, hoes and mattocks arose in many places, and hoe cultivation must have been common wherever farming was practiced. It is the traditional tillage of tropical and subtropical regions with stony soils, steep slopes, root crops and widely spaced coarse grains.

soil-agri-113.title: The mole plough, which drains a field from below
soil-agri-113.text: A mole plough builds a drain without digging a trench. This deep plough has a torpedo-shaped tip that leaves a drainage channel underground, or breaks up deep impermeable layers. Its bullet-shaped share forms a tunnel about 75 mm (3.0 in) across, and an expander presses the soil outward into a long-lasting channel. Mole drains lie up to 950 mm (37 in) deep at an angle to pipe drains, into which their water seeps and runs to a ditch. Heavy land needs such draining to bring its water content down to a level efficient for plant growth. A simple field test tells whether a subsoil suits moling. If a pencil pushed through a hand-compacted, tennis-ball-sized sample from moling depth leaves the ball unsplit, it does.

soil-agri-115.title: The cultivator, which stirs the soil around the crop
soil-agri-115.text: A harrow disturbs the whole soil surface, while a cultivator works in careful patterns that spare the crop plants. This farm implement for secondary tillage takes two forms. One is a frame with teeth dragged through the soil; the other is a machine with rotating disks or teeth, such as a rotary tiller. Before planting, it stirs and pulverizes soil to aerate it and prepare a smooth, loose bed for seeds. After the crop emerges, it kills weeds. Toothed cultivators resemble chisel ploughs, but their teeth work near the surface, while chisel shanks work deep to break hardened layers. Field cultivators also bury residue to help warm the soil, and mix the soil so the crop has enough water and nutrients.

soil-agri-122.title: Vertical tillage, a method without a settled definition
soil-agri-122.text: What counts as vertical tillage varies considerably, even among its proponents. Broadly, it is a set of tillage principles that, like {{ref:soil-agri-065}}, aims to improve soil health, raise infiltration and reduce erosion and compaction. It avoids inverting the soil and keeps residue on the surface. Small forward-facing discs slice the residue so it decomposes faster. It often adds a deep ripping tool to break hard pans and compaction left by traditional implements and heavy machinery such as combine harvesters. Its place is disputed. Proponents class it with no-till and with that wider approach, while detractors say its vigorous soil movement excludes it. The quarrel matters because US payments promote no-till.

soil-agri-125.title: The moisture at which soil crumbles best
soil-agri-125.text: Till a soil too wet or too dry and it comes up in large clods. The optimum water content for tillage is the soil moisture at which tillage breaks the soil into the largest number of small aggregates. Missing it damages structure and raises the readily dispersible clay content. The optimum can be related to the water content at the lower plastic limit; for several soils it equals 0.9 times the plastic limit. That link has limits. The plastic limit is measured on molded rather than undisturbed soil, and many sandy soils have no plastic limit. Friability, the tendency to crumble, peaks at the plastic limit. Yet many clay soils drain so slowly that they stay wetter than it unless plant roots draw the water out.

soil-agri-116.title: The seedbed, a seed's first home in the soil
soil-agri-116.text: The smaller the seed, the finer the soil it needs. A seedbed is the local soil environment into which seeds are planted. It should be loose and smooth, without large lumps, so seeds go in easily at the depth that germinates them best. Preparation breaks up compacted soil so air and water can enter and seedlings can push through. On farms, secondary tillage with harrows and cultivators usually does the work, perhaps after primary tillage with mouldboard or chisel ploughs. No-till skips this step. Organic matter such as compost or peat may be added to improve the seedbed's soil structure.

soil-agri-121.title: Minimum tillage: only as much as the crop needs
soil-agri-121.text: Minimum tillage avoids primary tillage entirely. This system for conserving soil keeps manipulation to the minimum a crop needs, without turning the soil over. Secondary tillage is practiced only to a small extent. The system also includes minimum furrowing, organic fertilizer, biological pest control and minimal use of chemicals. Some minimum or low-till methods mix tilled and untilled approaches, for example shallow disc harrowing without ploughing, or {{ref:soil-agri-120}}.

soil-agri-120.title: Strip-till: tilling only where the seed will go
soil-agri-120.text: Each tilled row is usually only about eight to ten inches wide. Strip-till is a minimum-tillage conservation system that tills just the narrow strip of soil that will hold the seed row, leaving the soil between rows untilled. It combines the soil drying and warming of conventional tillage with the soil protection of no-till. Also called zone tillage, it breaks up compacted layers under the row, prepares a seedbed and improves internal drainage. Breaking the crust lets air in and speeds organic matter decay, yet a two-year study found no change in organic carbon or extractable phosphorus. Fertilizer can be placed directly in the seed row during strip-tilling, so less is needed and it sits closer to the roots. Combined implements can cut field trips to two or even one, saving time and fuel and reducing compaction. Strip-till conserves more moisture than intensive tillage, though sometimes less than no-till, and its erosion is light by comparison with intensive tillage. At one low-phosphorus site it yielded 43.5 bushels/acre (2,925.5 kg/ha) against 41.5 bu/a (2,791 kg/ha) under no-till. Its yields match intensive tillage without the cost.

soil-agri-130.title: Controlled traffic farming: wheels stay in their lanes
soil-agri-130.text: Random traffic compacts about 75% of a field in one season and all of it by the second. Controlled traffic farming confines all machinery loads to the smallest possible area of permanent traffic lanes. A proper system cuts tracking to 15%, always in the same place. It needs matched implement and wheel track widths, with machines kept in the same lanes every year. That is easiest with RTK satellite guidance and auto-steer accurate to about ± 2 cm. Untracked soil gains porosity, infiltration and drainage, with less erosion and waterlogging and better rooting. Most adopters till little or not at all, because the structure no longer needs repair. The drawbacks are a high initial investment and the need for GPS guidance and adapted machines, but compacted soils can take more than 5 years to recover.

soil-agri-101.title: The plough pan, a hard floor made by tillage
soil-agri-101.text: Tillage that loosens the surface can harden the soil beneath it. A plough pan, also called a tillage pan, is a compacted layer of soil created by tillage. Continued cultivation and traffic create compacted, impermeable layers within the soil profile. Over-ploughing can form a hardpan, which farmers usually break with a subsoiler that slices through the hardened layer deep below the surface. Chisel ploughs and zone tillage are also used to break up plough pans.

soil-agri-112.title: Subsoiling: breaking hard layers below the plough's reach
soil-agri-112.text: Most tillage tools work the top 15–20 cm (6–8 in) of soil. A subsoiler loosens soil to twice that depth, usually 45–75 cm (18–30 in) or more. Subsoiling is deep tillage with this implement, whose heavy shanks break up soil below the depth reached by ploughs, harrows or rototillers. Angled wings on the shanks lift and shatter the hardpan that compaction builds, improving crop growth wherever compaction is a problem. Afterward, roots reach deeper moisture and nutrients in hot, dry seasons. In wet weather, water drains through the shattered zones, so crops are less likely to drown. The work is slow and power-hungry: pulling one point through hard soil takes 60 to 100 horsepower (45 to 75 kW). The shanks should reach 2.5–5 cm (1–2 in) below the deepest compacted layer. A subsoiler is not a mole plough, which cuts underground drainage channels. In-row subsoiling counts among the conservation tillage practices. On poorly drained land, deep tillage may substitute for costlier tile drainage. It may also be needed where a clay-enriched lower horizon becomes too compacted.

reviews.tillage-and-cultivation: Tillage loosens and aerates the topsoil and kills weeds, but it also degrades structure, speeds erosion and compacts the soil, sometimes into a plough pan. Its tools grew from the hoe and the ard to the heavy mouldboard plough, which turned the soil over, reshaped fields into long strips and made farming communal. In 1731 Jethro Tull argued that land could never be tilled too much, but scientific observation, and the Dust Bowl, showed the cost. The answer has been to till less and leave more crop residue on the surface: residue cover defines intensive, reduced and conservation tillage, and no-till never tills at all. Each step trades one problem for another, from slower spring warming to more herbicide, and researchers still disagree over how much carbon no-till really stores.
